script.analysis: All 18,234 canonical characters read without truncation and hash verified. Three matched $100K personas open a 30-year $986K mystery; a week-six unsolicited offer is withheld as the explanation. Chronological progression follows home-rich Denise liquidity trouble, Wes advisor coffee and financing envelopes, truck/contribution pause, autumn market stress, year-three fee folder, year-five Omar tax-plan click and year-30 reconciliation. Repeated folder/coffee/envelope motifs connect scenes; a late reveal makes the truck/paused deposits larger than the visible advisor cost. A community promotion precedes tax details and the conclusion returns to a four-minute liquidity action. This is stronger narrative construction than a disconnected list, but invented causal sequencing, inaccurate combined endpoint and omitted Roth mechanics weaken its promise of honest nonstacked math. Audio, edits and retention remain unverified.

claim_audit: Denise/Omar/Wes and the precisely sequenced marketing contacts are illustrative narratives, not verified longitudinal households. There is no evidence that crossing exactly $100K caused a phone call, preapproval, credit tier or 30-year result. Advisor minimums vary; credit underwriting is not determined by net worth alone. Boring index holdings do not make an investor invisible to commercial incentives.

SCF 2022 mean family net worth $1,063,700 and median $192,900 are supported, in 2022 dollars. Using the scripts rounded $1,063,000, the ratio is 5.51, not three and a half. A roughly 38th-percentile $100K balance requires an identified weighted distribution and date; it also contradicts describing Denise at $104K as wealthier than 60% of the country. Family/household statistics must not silently become individual percentiles or current nominal values.

$100K at an assumed 7% real return produces $7K expected annual growth in a deterministic illustration, not guaranteed cash income. Equity returns and principal fluctuate. Three index funds can overlap rather than diversify. The 68%-in-primary-residence claim requires population/denominator and does not describe every median family. Maintenance at 1%, $4K implied house value and 8%-10% exit cost vary; equity can sometimes be borrowed against but adds debt/call/default costs, so permanently inaccessible is too absolute.

The main fee example reproduces with annual stated rates divided by 12 and end-month deposits: $100K plus $1K/month for 30 years at 7% gives $2,031,621; at 6%, $1,606,773; gap $424,848. These are scenario conventions, not forecasts. If 7% means effective annual real return, results are about $1.931M and $1.549M instead. Fee deduction timing is simplified; a 1% asset charge is not exactly subtracting one percentage point under every convention. Advice value and an hourly $2K price are not guaranteed equivalent.

The combined Wes schedule does NOT reproduce under the same monthly convention: $100K growing for 30 years at 6%, no deposits for five years, then $600/month for 25 years gives $1,018,054, not $1,046,000. Relative to Omar the gap is $1,013,567, not $986K. Applying the fee last gives $279,639 fee effect, close to $280K, but the other effects total $733,928, not $705K. Attribution is order-dependent, not a uniquely identified causal partition. The valid warning against adding overlapping costs does not repair the wrong combined endpoint.

The first-five-years $1K monthly deposit pause costs about $409,899 at the final 30-year horizon with 7%/12 monthly growth. The earlier ~$476K claim needs a different retirement horizon/convention: a 33-year horizon at 7% effective annual yields about $473K. Retirement age is not specified there. Its later $410K is consistent with 30-year monthly compounding. A permanent $400/month reduction for all 30 years alone costs about $487,988 at 7%/12; the stated $419K standalone truck loss needs an explicit different schedule. Trade-in negative-equity shares cannot establish the same borrowers will renew payments forever.

IRS supports 2026 regular elective deferral $24,500, IRA $7,500 and defined-contribution additions cap $72K, subject to compensation and plan conditions; employer money uses cap space. Non-Roth after-tax contributions are not automatically Roth. Mega-backdoor treatment requires permitted contributions plus a qualifying conversion/rollover, with pre-tax earnings potentially taxable; availability is unrelated to an exact net-worth threshold. IRA/Roth eligibility, deduction/income and access limits apply.

IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-19 supports HSA $4,400 self-only/$8,750 family for eligible coverage, with other eligibility and contribution conditions. Qualified medical distributions and contribution treatment are conditional; using an HSA for prescriptions is legitimate. Triple tax advantage is generally a federal description and not universal state treatment. Clicking a contribution option cannot move an existing $100K into tax shelters instantly beyond annual limits.

The standalone tax scenario reproduces: $100K x 1.07^25 = $542,743; x 1.05^25 = $338,635; gap $204,108. A fixed two-point tax drag is assumed, not intrinsic to all taxable investing. Deferral can leave tax on traditional withdrawals; Roth conversion costs/qualified distribution conditions and tax-efficient taxable holdings alter comparisons. The script switches from 7% real in the narrative to 7% gross in this example, leaving purchasing-power comparability unclear.

Bessembinders university summary supports about 26K U.S. stocks, 1926-2016, and 86 firms producing about half of wealth creation above Treasury bills; this is historical concentration evidence, not proof every stock picker loses. Hartford primary page supports 78% best-day clustering for a specified 1995-2024 window; it does not prove timing is mathematically impossible for every investor. Excluding only best days is a hindsight counterfactual, not a symmetric trading model; the exact $71,750/$32,871/missing-60 figures and seven-of-ten proximity were not independently reproduced.

Morningstar Mind the Gap 2025 measures dollar- versus time-weighted outcomes over a defined decade; its retrieved PDF does not substantiate the exact 8.7%/9.9% overall pair. Even a valid gap is not all a tax on flinching: contribution/withdrawal timing and fund mix matter, and necessary cash flows are not mistakes. It cannot establish every advisor causes the modeled fee loss or cures a measured behavioral gap.

Bankrate emergency percentages need exact wording/sample dates: could pay from savings, would pay from savings and without debt are distinct. Redfin equity, Boston Fed marginal-propensity ratio, vehicle price/payment and underwater trade-in percentages, 40% 84-month loans and 16% catch-up use lack matched original sources here. Catch-up eligibility is age-based and cannot establish whether a 32-year-old ever restores saving. Denise $551K house plus $675K liquid totals $1.226M and 55.1% liquid, but no complete house/debt/return/contribution schedule produces it. Liquid invested assets are not necessarily cash spendable without selling.
